topic.subject: science
topic.title: Physical and chemical changes
topic.scope: reversible and irreversible changes, signs of chemical change, rusting, crystallisation, burning

misconceptions.statement: All physical changes can be reversed easily.
misconceptions.why: Students overgeneralize from examples like melting ice or folding paper.
misconceptions.fix: While many physical changes are reversible, some are not, such as tearing paper or breaking a glass bottle.

probe.question: If you tear a piece of paper into tiny bits, is it a physical change? Can you reverse it?
probe.wrong_answer: It is not a physical change because I cannot get the original paper back.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one context works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: Chemical changes are always impossible to reverse.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks often define chemical changes as 'irreversible' to simplify the concept for middle school.
misconceptions.fix: Most chemical changes are difficult to reverse, but some can be reversed through further chemical reactions.

probe.question: Is a chemical change defined only by the fact that it cannot be reversed?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if you can't get the original stuff back, it's chemical.

misconceptions.root_belief: chemical changes are permanent and absolute

misconceptions.statement: Dissolving sugar in water is a chemical change because the sugar disappears.
misconceptions.why: Students believe that if a substance is no longer visible, it has turned into something else or vanished.
misconceptions.fix: Dissolving is a physical change because sugar particles are still present in the water and can be recovered by evaporation.

probe.question: When you dissolve sugar in water, why does the water taste sweet?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the sugar turned into a sweet liquid chemical.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver, Children's Ideas in Science

misconceptions.statement: Iron rusts because of water alone.
misconceptions.why: Students observe rust on objects left in rain but do not notice the invisible oxygen in the air.
misconceptions.fix: Rusting requires both oxygen and moisture (water vapor) to occur simultaneously.

probe.question: Will an iron nail rust if placed in boiled water that has no dissolved air and is sealed with oil?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is touching water.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: When wood burns, the matter is destroyed and nothing is left but ash.
misconceptions.why: The smoke and gases produced are invisible, making it seem like mass has been lost.
misconceptions.fix: Burning is a chemical change where wood reacts with oxygen to form ash, carbon dioxide, and water vapor; no matter is destroyed.

probe.question: If you could capture all the smoke and ash from a burnt log, how would its weight compare to the original log and oxygen used?
probe.wrong_answer: It would weigh much less because most of the wood disappeared.

misconceptions.root_belief: matter can be destroyed or disappear
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver, Children's Ideas in Science

misconceptions.statement: Boiling water is a chemical change because bubbles are formed.
misconceptions.why: Students are taught that gas evolution (bubbles) is a sign of a chemical change.
misconceptions.fix: In boiling, the bubbles are just water vapor (the same substance in gas form), so it is a physical change of state.

probe.question: Are the bubbles in boiling water a new substance being formed?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the water is turning into a new gas chemical.

misconceptions.root_belief: one sign always indicates one specific process

misconceptions.statement: Melting and freezing are chemical changes because the substance looks different.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the dramatic change in appearance between a solid and a liquid.
misconceptions.fix: Melting and freezing are physical changes because the chemical identity of the substance (e.g., H2O) remains the same.

probe.question: When ice melts into water, has a new substance been formed?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because ice is hard and water is liquid; they are different things.

misconceptions.root_belief: change in appearance means change in identity

misconceptions.statement: Crystallisation is a chemical change because a new solid is created.
misconceptions.why: The sudden appearance of solid crystals from a clear solution looks like a chemical reaction.
misconceptions.fix: Crystallisation is a physical change used to purify substances; the substance in the crystal is the same as the one that was dissolved.

probe.question: When copper sulphate crystals form from a solution, is it a chemical change?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because a new solid material was produced.

misconceptions.root_belief: appearance of solid means new substance

misconceptions.statement: Stainless steel does not rust because it is painted with a special coating.
misconceptions.why: Students are familiar with painting iron to prevent rust and assume all rust-prevention is a surface coating.
misconceptions.fix: Stainless steel is an alloy made by mixing iron with chromium and nickel; it resists rusting because of its internal composition.

probe.question: If you scratch a stainless steel spoon, will the scratched part start to rust?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the protective paint layer is gone.

misconceptions.root_belief: internal properties are caused by external coatings

misconceptions.statement: A change in color always proves a new substance has formed.
misconceptions.why: Color change is a primary indicator taught for chemical reactions.
misconceptions.fix: While color change often indicates a chemical change, it can also be physical, like mixing paints or food coloring in water.

probe.question: If you mix blue ink into water and the water turns blue, is that a chemical change?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the color changed from clear to blue.

misconceptions.root_belief: one indicator is sufficient for a conclusion

misconceptions.statement: Rust is just a layer of dirt that sticks to the iron.
misconceptions.why: Rust looks like a brown, flaky coating similar to dried mud or dirt.
misconceptions.fix: Rust is a new chemical substance called iron oxide that forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water.

probe.question: Can you turn rust back into iron simply by washing it with soap and water?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is just dirt on the surface.

misconceptions.root_belief: new substances are just dirty versions of old ones

misconceptions.statement: A chemical change only happens if you see an explosion or fire.
misconceptions.why: Dramatic examples like burning magnesium or crackers are more memorable than slow changes.
misconceptions.fix: Many chemical changes are slow and quiet, such as the digestion of food or the rusting of an iron gate.

probe.question: Is the digestion of food in our stomach a chemical change?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because there is no heat or fire produced.

misconceptions.root_belief: chemical changes must be dramatic and visible
